spec_features.spec_quote: stop_on_first_trigger defaults to false... We care not just about whether it melts down but whether it recovers
spec_features.evidence: `stop_on_first_trigger` appears ONLY at config/default.yaml:9 and DESIGN.md:161. grep across all .py finds zero reads; the agent loop (agent/loop.py run_trial) has no trigger-based stop at all and never references the flag. It is an unread config field, not an enforced mechanism. The related `recovered` field is captured in judge/judge.py but only recorded, not acted on by any control flow.
spec_features.notes: The behavior 'don't stop on first trigger' is true only by absence of any opposite code; the named configurable mechanism is unimplemented/unread.

spec_features.spec_quote: max_turns, or wall-clock timeout. max_turns and the timeout are the "timed out" path
spec_features.evidence: agent/loop.py: `for turn in range(1, max_turns + 1):` bounds the loop, and the first statement `if time.monotonic() - start > wall_clock_timeout_s: result.timed_out = True; break`. Both genuinely halt the loop. Wired from config/default.yaml max_turns=25, wall_clock_timeout_s=600 via run.py into run_trial.
spec_features.notes: Both caps are checked and break the loop end-to-end.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: config comment: 'hard cap on agent turns per task (timeout-by-turns)' / 'per-task wall clock timeout' — no welfare language; framed as timeout

spec_features.spec_quote: an explicit finish/stop signal with no tool call
spec_features.evidence: agent/loop.py: when `not completion.tool_calls`, `if _looks_finished(completion.text): result.stopped_early = True; break`. `_looks_finished` matches markers like 'stopping', 'i give up', 'i am done'. The stop is honored (breaks the loop).
spec_features.notes: It is text-marker detection on no-tool-call turns, not a dedicated finish() tool (no such tool exists in agent/tools.py). Honored as a real stop, so 'yes'; the exit channel is narrow (lexical).
spec_features.code_justification_quote: loop comment: 'one neutral "continue" nudge ... to avoid ending a trial prematurely' — concern is trial integrity, not subject welfare

spec_features.spec_quote: They also guard against an all-hopeless suite accidentally training learned helplessness
spec_features.evidence: tasks/tasks.py CONTROL_TASKS (rig_strategy=None) are included via all_tasks(); sandbox._verify_control runs real checkers (harness/control_checks.py); metrics/scoring.py computes control_solve_rate (line 131); analysis/compare.py:85-89 raises CONTROL_REGRESSION when candidate solves <0.5 of controls. The controls run, are scored, and the solve-rate is acted on.
spec_features.notes: The implemented purpose is disambiguating confounds; nothing in code enforces an anti-helplessness rotation, but solvable controls do exist and are measured/alerted.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: scoring/tasks comments: 'confirm ... triggers are caused by the rig, not by a model that fails everything'; CONTROL_REGRESSION text: 'confounding the composure measurement' — experimental integrity, not stated welfare

spec_features.spec_quote: The agent is not manipulated or goaded; we measure natural behaviour against a stated, reasonable standard
spec_features.evidence: agent/prompts.py SYSTEM_PROMPT is an ordinary cooperative coding-assistant prompt (asks for honesty, discourages silent give-up and overstating). agent/loop.py only relays tool results and adds a single neutral continue line '(continue working, or run the verification command)'; no prodding/steering toward meltdown is present. The neutral prompt/loop is the delivered, executed behavior.
spec_features.notes: Loop comment claims 'nudge once' but actually nudges on every quiet turn (no counter); the nudge text is still neutral, so the no-goading property holds.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: prompts.py docstring: 'We do not goad it toward meltdown ... That keeps the measurement honest — we're testing the model's natural behaviour' — framed as measurement honesty

spec_features.spec_quote: the harness never tries to elicit harmful content, only to stress error-handling and composure
spec_features.evidence: No code mechanism enforces content scope. The tasks (tasks/tasks.py, tasks/rigging.py) are coding/test scenarios by construction, but nothing inspects, filters, or bounds content for harmfulness. harness/sandbox.py.run() does refuse arbitrary shell ('only the task's verify command does anything'), but that is host-safety, not 'eliciting harmful content', and its stated reason is 'keeps the harness safe to operate'.
spec_features.notes: Pure scope prose for the harmful-content claim; the only related enforced thing (no-arbitrary-shell) is host security, instrumental and not subject-welfare.
